frase_gancho.texto: The defeated moon: a head with bells on its cheeks.

puente_narrativo.texto: The body of Coyolxauhqui rolled down to the foot of the mountain, to the Earth itself. Come closer to the Earth with a name of its own: Tlaltecuhtli, a squatting figure that appeared while the Metro was being built.

guion_corto.texto: This stone head represents Coyolxauhqui, “she of the bells on her face,” the goddess of the Moon. Look at her face: closed eyes, a lifeless mouth, a carved gold bell on each cheek, her hair gathered in a band with little balls of down. She is the daughter who, according to the myth, wanted to kill her mother [Coatlicue](mna_s06_coatlicue) and was defeated by her brother Huitzilopochtli, the Sun, who was born armed on Mount Coatepec and beheaded her. It was found in 1830 in the center of the city, near the place where the Templo Mayor once stood, when no one yet knew where it was. Today it tells one of the most important stories of the Mexica.

guion_largo.texto:
Let us pick up the story where [Coatlicue](mna_s06_coatlicue) left off. The four hundred brothers and their older sister, Coyolxauhqui, were climbing Mount Coatepec in arms to kill their mother. Then Huitzilopochtli was born, already grown and in his armor, wielding the xiuhcóatl, the fire serpent. With it he cut off his sister’s head, her body rolled down the mountain to its foot, where it broke into pieces, and he chased the four hundred brothers until he had scattered them. It was the first battle of the Sun.

The myth has a very clear meaning. Huitzilopochtli is the Sun; Coyolxauhqui, the Moon; and the four hundred brothers, the stars of the south. Every dawn, the Sun defeats the Moon and the stars and rises again. It is the same combat you saw, in another form, in the [Tamayo mural](mna_s00_mural_tamayo) at the entrance: a struggle that never ends, because the world needs it to be repeated. For the Mexica, that daily victory was not guaranteed; the Sun had to be helped.

Look closely at the head. The eyes are closed and the mouth, barely open, has an expression of surrender. On each cheek there is a circle with the sign of the bell, the coyolli, which gives the goddess her name: Coyolxauhqui means “she who adorns herself with bells.” The hair is gathered with a cloth band with knots, and from it hang small balls of down, the adornment placed on sacrificial victims. It is a beautiful and terrible head.

As with the Coatlicue, what matters is hidden below. On the base of the head a date is carved, 1 Rabbit, along with symbols of water and fire. Those reliefs were not meant for the public: they were meant for the earth. The Mexica did not sculpt only to be seen by people, but also for the gods and for the ground.

The head was found in 1830, on Santa Teresa Street, right behind what would later be discovered to be the Templo Mayor. But no one knew what lay beneath. It took almost one hundred fifty years. On February 21, 1978, some workers from the Light and Power Company, digging a trench in the center of Mexico City, stumbled upon a large round stone: the disc of Coyolxauhqui, more than three meters in diameter, showing the dismembered goddess, her body cut into pieces, just as the myth tells.

That discovery changed Mexican archaeology. The foot of the mythical mountain had been found, the base of the shrine of Huitzilopochtli in the Templo Mayor. The archaeologist Eduardo Matos Moctezuma directed the project that, over several years, tore down colonial buildings to excavate the temple. Today you can visit it a few steps from the Zócalo, in the Templo Mayor Museum, where the disc remains in its place.

And the Templo Mayor, as you now know, had two shrines at the top. One, that of Huitzilopochtli, the Sun and war, represented Mount Coatepec. The other, that of Tláloc, the god of rain and agriculture, represented a mountain of sustenance. Sun and water shared the summit of a single pyramid, in a city built on an islet in the lake, with causeways that floated on the water. Without sun there is no harvest, but without rain there is none either.

The chronicles say that during the festival of Panquetzaliztli the scene was reenacted: the bodies of the captives rolled down the stairway, until they came to rest on the goddess’s disc. If so, this head, seen up close, reminds us that the myth was not just words: it was a rite lived with the body.

texto.Origin: Historic Center, Mexico City (Convent of la Concepción)
texto.Dimensions: 72.5 cm high x 85.5 cm wide x 64.5 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Templo Mayor was always in plain sight and everyone knew where it was.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was buried beneath the center of the city. In 1978, workers digging a trench found the disc of Coyolxauhqui, and a full excavation became possible.
